title: SYE TE1 Practice Mock Exam (90 min, 58 pts)
description: Full-length English TE1 practice exam modeled after the HEIG-VD SYE TE1 format: Architecture & Interrupts, Process States & Context Switch, fork()/waitpid() Tracing, Threads & Memory Map, 2-Pipe IPC, Signals & Sockets, and CPU Scheduling.

sources.title: SYE TE1 Exam Supplement
sources.notes: High-yield traps, sequence tracing, memory maps, and 2-pipe IPC

sections.title: Part 1: Architecture, Memory & Interrupts (14 pts)
sections.description: Closed-book style questions on byte-addressable RAM, hardware/software interrupts, and syscall mechanics.

blocks.title: Q1–Q2 (4 pts): RAM Region & Address Space
blocks.prompt:
A 32-bit system has RAM mapped from `0x0040'0000` to `0x00BF'FFFF` (inclusive).

1. **(2 pts)** What is the exact size of this RAM region (in MiB / KiB)?
2. **(2 pts)** What is the maximum addressable space of this 32-bit CPU (in GiB), and why?
self_check_criteria: Computed size = 0x00BF'FFFF - 0x0040'0000 + 1 = 0x0080'0000 bytes.
Stated max 32-bit address space = 2^32 bytes = 4 GiB because address registers are 32 bits wide and memory is byte-addressable.
blocks.model_answer:
1) Size = 0x00BF'FFFF - 0x0040'0000 + 1 = 0x0080'0000 bytes = 8 * 16^5 = 8 * 2^20 bytes = 8 MiB.
2) Max address space = 2^32 bytes = 4 GiB, because each byte has a unique 32-bit address (0x0000'0000 to 0xFFFF'FFFF).

blocks.title: Q3–Q5 (6 pts): Hardware IRQs, Software Interrupts & Timer
blocks.prompt:
3. **(2 pts)** Describe the hardware/OS steps when a device raises a hardware interrupt (IRQ).
4. **(2 pts)** Name three distinct types of software interrupts.
5. **(2 pts)** "The hardware timer sends an IRQ to the CPU." Explain what happens at the **software level** (both kernel side and user side).
self_check_criteria: Q3: Device -> Interrupt Controller (APIC) -> CPU finishes current instruction & switches to Kernel Mode -> looks up Interrupt Vector -> executes ISR -> acknowledges IRQ & restores task in User Mode.
Q4: (1) Syscall instruction (svc/int 0x80/syscall), (2) Arithmetic/execution fault (div-by-zero, illegal instruction), (3) Memory/alignment fault (invalid address / segfault).

Q5: Kernel side: Timer ISR updates ticks/quantum, calls schedule(); if quantum expired, context switch (Running->Ready, next Ready->Running). User side: interrupted process is transparently paused and later resumes unaware.
blocks.model_answer:
3) Device asserts IRQ -> APIC prioritizes & signals CPU -> CPU finishes current instruction, enters Kernel Mode, uses Interrupt Vector to jump to ISR -> ISR handles/acknowledges IRQ -> restores saved state and returns to User Mode.
4) Syscall instruction (svc/int 0x80), arithmetic/execution error (divide by zero, illegal instruction), memory/alignment fault (segfault).
5) Kernel side: Timer ISR runs, decrements quantum, invokes schedule(); if quantum=0, saves outgoing PCB (Running->Ready) and restores next process PCB (Ready->Running). User side: running app is paused transparently without knowing it was interrupted.

blocks.title: Q6 (1 pt): Orphan & Zombie States
blocks.question: True or False: An orphan process can enter the `Zombie` state.
blocks.explanation: True! An orphan is reparented to `init` (`PID 1`). When the orphan later calls `exit()`, it enters the `Zombie` state until `init` reaps it with `waitpid()`.
hints: What happens when an adopted orphan finishes executing?

blocks.title: Q7 (1 pt): Object Code
blocks.question: True or False: Object code (`.o`) produced by the compiler is a complete executable binary.
blocks.explanation: False! Object code contains unresolved symbolic addresses and lacks linked libraries and `crt` startup code. The **linker** produces the executable binary (e.g., ELF).
hints: What tool resolves calls like printf() into an ELF executable?

blocks.title: Q8 (2 pts): System Call Properties
blocks.question: A system call... (Select all that apply)
options: ...requires passing arguments between user space and kernel space.
...uses a single interrupt vector shared across all system calls.
...is wrapped by a C stub function in user space.
correct_answer: ...requires passing arguments between user space and kernel space.
...uses a single interrupt vector shared across all system calls.
...is wrapped by a C stub function in user space.
blocks.explanation: Syscalls are **synchronous** software interrupts (not asynchronous). They pass syscall number + args via the ABI, share a single software interrupt vector (e.g., `svc` / `int 0x80`), and are invoked via C stub functions in `libc`.
hints: Are software interrupts synchronous or asynchronous?

sections.title: Part 2: Process Management & Context Switching (10 pts)
sections.description: State transitions, PCB contents, process vs. thread context switch, and mode switch traps.

blocks.title: Q9–Q11 (7 pts): State Trace, PCB & Context Switch Cost
blocks.prompt:
9. **(3 pts)** A process enters the system, is preempted once by the scheduler, then blocks on an I/O request, and finally terminates. List **every state and transition** in order (assume 2 processes in the system).
10. **(2 pts)** What is a PCB and what is its role?
11. **(2 pts)** What does a **process** context switch involve compared to a **thread** context switch?
self_check_criteria: Q9: New -> Ready -> Running -> Ready (preempted) -> Running -> Waiting (I/O) -> Ready (I/O done, never Waiting->Running!) -> Running -> Zombie -> Terminated.
Q10: Kernel-only data structure ('ID card') storing PID, state, PC/registers, SP, address space, open FDs, exit code; used during context switches.

Q11: Process switch saves/restores PCB, flushes/syncs caches, and reconfigures the MMU (different virtual address spaces). Thread switch only swaps TCB (PC, registers, SP) within the same address space (no MMU reconfiguration).
blocks.model_answer:
9) New -> Ready -> Running -> Ready (preemption) -> Running -> Waiting (I/O request) -> Ready (I/O complete) -> Running -> Zombie (exit) -> Freed (waitpid).
10) Process Control Block: kernel-only structure holding process state, PID, registers/PC/SP, memory context, open FDs, and exit code.
11) Process context switch requires saving/restoring PCB, syncing caches, and reconfiguring the MMU; thread context switch shares the same address space/MMU and only swaps TCB registers/SP/PC.

blocks.title: Q12 (1 pt): Mode Switch vs. Context Switch
blocks.question: True or False: A CPU execution mode switch automatically causes a context switch.
blocks.explanation: False! Entering Kernel Mode for a syscall or IRQ returns to the *same* process if no rescheduling occurs—a mode switch with zero context switch.
hints: Does every syscall switch to a different process?

blocks.title: Q13 (2 pts): PCB Properties
blocks.question: A process PCB... (Select all that apply)
options: ...is used during context switches between processes.
...is used during a CPU mode switch.
...contains information about all currently running processes.
...contains a reference to the process's heap.
correct_answer: ...is used during context switches between processes.
...contains a reference to the process's heap.
blocks.explanation: Each process has its *own* PCB (not a global list of all processes). It is used for process context switches and stores memory pointers including the heap, whereas a pure CPU mode switch does not swap PCBs.
hints: Is there one PCB per process or one PCB for the whole OS?

sections.title: Part 3: Process Creation — fork() & waitpid() (16 pts)
sections.description: Trace a 2-iteration fork() + waitpid() loop, draw the sequence diagram, and analyze orphans/zombies.

blocks.title: Part 3 C Program to Trace
Q14–Q17 (16 pts): Sequence Diagram, Outputs, Orphans & Zombies
blocks.prompt:
14. **(10 pts)** Draw the full sequence diagram showing all processes (`P0`, `P1`, ...), `fork()`, `waitpid()`, `printf()`, and `exit()`.
15. **(2 pts)** List all possible console outputs.
16. **(2 pts)** Are there any orphan processes? Justify.
17. **(2 pts)** Can any process enter the `Zombie` state here, and if so, until when?
self_check_criteria: Identified 4 processes total: P0, P1 (child of P0 at i=0), P2 (child of P1 at i=1), P3 (child of P0 at i=1).
Traced exact deterministic output: val = 4, val = 6, val = 14, val = 21.
Q16: No orphans, because every parent calls waitpid() on every child before exiting.
Q17: Yes, a child enters Zombie when it calls exit() until its parent's waitpid() collects its exit code and frees its PCB.
blocks.model_answer:
14-15) P0(val=1) forks P1(val=2) and waits. P1 forks P2(val=4) and waits. P2 prints 'val = 4' and calls exit(4). P1 wakes (status=4, val=2+4=6), prints 'val = 6', calls exit(6). P0 wakes (status=6, val=1+6=7), loops i=1, forks P3(val=14) and waits. P3 prints 'val = 14', calls exit(14). P0 wakes (status=14, val=7+14=21), prints 'val = 21', calls exit(21). Only 1 output order is possible: 4, 6, 14, 21.
16) No orphans: every parent waits for its children via waitpid().
17) Yes: each child is briefly a Zombie between its exit() call and its parent's waitpid() returning and freeing its PCB.

sections.title: Part 4: Processes, Threads & Memory Map (11 pts)
sections.description: Analyze a multi-process, multi-threaded C program, buffer sharing, process states, and virtual memory sections.

blocks.title: Part 4 C Program to Analyze
Q18–Q22 (11 pts): Process/Thread Tree, Buffer Sharing, States & Memory Map
blocks.prompt:
18. **(2 pts)** Sketch the process/thread hierarchy of this application.
19. **(2 pts)** Do all threads share the same `log_buf` buffer? Justify.
20. **(3 pts)** Suppose the parent is currently **`Running`** at Line 22 (`pthread_create(&workers[2], ...)`). In what state(s) can the child process be? Justify each case.
21. **(3 pts)** Draw the virtual memory sections of the **child** process (high to low addresses), clearly showing all stacks and where `req_id` and `log_buf` (both pointer and allocated bytes) live.
22. **(1 pt)** Can there be orphan processes or threads? Justify.
self_check_criteria: Q18: Parent P0 (main + T2); Child P1 (main + T0, T1).
Q19: No across processes (P0 and P1 have separate virtual address spaces after fork()); YES within P1 (T0 and T1 share the same Heap log_buf!).

Q20: Child P1 can be Ready (created/running earlier, waiting for CPU), Running (on another core in SMP), Waiting (blocked in sleep(5) or pthread_join), or Zombie (already finished and exited before parent called waitpid!).
Q21: High->Low: 3 Stacks (main, T0, T1) with req_id on T0/T1 stacks; Free space; Heap (4096B malloc buffer); .bss (log_buf pointer & workers[]); .data (string literals); .text.
Q22: No orphan processes (parent calls waitpid) and no orphan threads (both processes join their threads before exit).
blocks.model_answer:
18) P0 has main + workers[2]; P1 has main + workers[0], workers[1].
19) P0 and P1 have separate copies of log_buf (fork duplicates address space), but within P1, workers[0] and workers[1] share the same Heap log_buf (race condition!).
20) If parent is Running at Line 22, child P1 may be: Ready (scheduled after fork, waiting for CPU), Running (simultaneously on a 2nd core), Waiting (blocked in sleep(5) or pthread_join), or Zombie (already called exit(0) before parent reached waitpid).
21) High->Low: Stack(main), Stack(T0 with req_id), Stack(T1 with req_id), Free space, Heap (4096B buffer), .bss (log_buf ptr, workers[]), .data, .text.
22) No orphan processes (waitpid) and no orphan threads (pthread_join).

sections.title: Part 5 & 6: 2-Pipe IPC, Signals, Sockets & Scheduling (17 pts)
sections.description: Bidirectional 2-pipe C coding, signals/sockets True-False, and a quick scheduling check.

blocks.title: Q23 (6 pts): Bidirectional 2-Pipe IPC in C
blocks.prompt: Process A must send a `msg` (`len < 256` bytes) to Process B via an anonymous pipe. Process B must convert every lowercase ASCII letter to uppercase (or copy it to `reply_buf`) and send it back to Process A via a second anonymous pipe. Write the C function `void roundtrip_pipe(char *msg, int len)`.
self_check_criteria: Created 2 pipes (p_a2b[2], p_b2a[2]) BEFORE fork().
Closed unused ends in both parent and child.
Child reads from p_a2b[0], transforms/copies, writes to p_b2a[1], closes FDs, calls exit(0).
Parent writes to p_a2b[1], reads reply from p_b2a[0], closes FDs, calls waitpid().
blocks.model_answer: int p_a2b[2], p_b2a[2]; char reply[256]; pipe(p_a2b); pipe(p_b2a); pid_t pid = fork(); if (pid == 0) { close(p_a2b[1]); close(p_b2a[0]); int n = read(p_a2b[0], reply, len); for (int i=0; i<n; i++) if (reply[i]>='a' && reply[i]<='z') reply[i]-=32; write(p_b2a[1], reply, n); close(p_a2b[0]); close(p_b2a[1]); exit(0); } else { close(p_a2b[0]); close(p_b2a[1]); write(p_a2b[1], msg, len); read(p_b2a[0], reply, len); close(p_a2b[1]); close(p_b2a[0]); waitpid(pid, NULL, 0); }

blocks.title: Q24 (1 pt): Signals & Hardware Interrupts
blocks.question: True or False: Sending a POSIX signal from one process to another requires a hardware interrupt.
blocks.explanation: False! Signals are software events delivered by the kernel (e.g., via the `kill()` syscall), not hardware IRQs.
hints: Is kill() a hardware device or a syscall?

blocks.title: Q25 (1 pt): Masking Signals
blocks.question: True or False: A process can mask a signal so that it is deferred and delivered later when unmasked.
blocks.explanation: True! Masking a signal holds it pending until the process unmasks it (except `SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP`, which cannot be masked).
hints: What is the difference between masking and ignoring (SIG_IGN)?

blocks.title: Q26 (1 pt): Pending Signal Queue
blocks.question: True or False: Standard POSIX signals are queued so that 5 identical pending `SIGINT` signals will invoke the handler 5 times.
blocks.explanation: False! At most **one** pending occurrence of a given signal type is stored; duplicates while pending are coalesced.
hints: Recall C7: what happens if you press Ctrl+C multiple times before the process runs?

blocks.title: Q27 (1 pt): TCP/IP Sockets as IPC
blocks.question: True or False: A TCP/IP socket (e.g., over `127.0.0.1`) can be used as an IPC mechanism.
blocks.explanation: True! Sockets are part of the IPC subsystem and work both over networks and locally via loopback (`127.0.0.1`).
hints: Can two processes on the same machine talk over localhost?

blocks.title: Q28 (1 pt): Named Pipes & fork()
blocks.question: True or False: A named pipe (`mkfifo()`) requires `fork()` so unrelated processes can share it.
blocks.explanation: False! That is true for **anonymous** pipes (`pipe()`). A **named pipe (FIFO)** exists as a path in the filesystem, so any unrelated process can `open()` it.
hints: Why does a named pipe have a filename in the filesystem?

blocks.title: Q29 (1 pt): TCP Addressing
blocks.question: True or False: In TCP/IP, IP addresses alone are sufficient to identify the sending and receiving applications.
blocks.explanation: False! IP identifies the host machine; **TCP port numbers** are also required to identify the specific application/socket.
hints: What identifies a specific server on 192.168.1.34:8080?

blocks.title: Q30 (5 pts bonus): Round Robin Quantum Trade-off
blocks.question: In Round Robin scheduling, what happens if the time quantum $q$ is set **much smaller** than the context-switch duration?
options: CPU efficiency collapses because most CPU time is spent in kernel context-switching overhead
Round Robin behaves identically to FCFS
Processes transition directly from Waiting to Running
blocks.correct_answer: CPU efficiency collapses because most CPU time is spent in kernel context-switching overhead
blocks.explanation: A tiny quantum causes constant timer preemptions and context switches, wasting CPU cycles in kernel overhead. Conversely, a huge quantum makes RR behave like FCFS.
hints: What happens when context-switch time dominates useful user execution time?
